newsitem.title: UK: UK's Labour to follow gas deregulation timetable.
newsitem.headline: UK's Labour to follow gas deregulation timetable.

text.p: The UK's Labour Party plans to stick to the current timetable for the introduction of full domestic gas deregulation throughout Britain in 1998 if it forms a government, but will not follow it "slavishly", the party's energy spokesman said on Tuesday.
John Battle , opposition Labour's Energy spokesman told an industry conference that Labour must keep up the pressure to meet the timetable in 1998.
"We want no backsliding on that. But we are more concerned with getting it right than adhering slavishly to a timetable just because it's been set - but we still think the timetable is achievable".

All domestic natural gas consumers in Britain are scheduled to have the right to buy gas from any licensed supplier at an unspecified date in 1998. This follows a test in a pilot area of some 500,000 customers in Devon, Cornwall and Somerset this year, with a further test involving another 1.5 million customers in southern and western parts of England next year.

Battle said Labour has no intention of turning the clock back on the market deregulation that has taken place so far in Britain. "We welcome competition, if necessary we will promote it, and if necessary we will promote tougher regulation", he said.

But he added that in future the debate will focus on the relationship between competition policy and regulation. "There are two challenges: the introduction of competition to energy supplies must benefit all, not just a few.
"And we must confront the environmental challenge and not prejudice future generations."

Battle sees problems with the way competition has been introduced so far, with the Network Code -- the rules for shippers using the National Transmission System or trunk pipeline network -- coming in for criticism.

"The Network Code was set up late at night after much difficulty and signed at the last moment", he said. It was already showing signs of strain, he added. "Claims validation procedures are still chaotic. Producers are not giving accurate information about production which makes it impossible to track gas flows".

Battle said Labour believes opening the European market to British-style competition is crucial if the U.K. market is not to be at a disadvantage after 1998, when the Bacton-Zeebrugge gas interconnector pipeline allows gas to flow between British and European markets.

"Third party access to European networks is needed, a loosening of networks in Europe is needed", he said. "The (Irish) EU presidency wanted to introduce a one-off proposal to allow access to pipelines (at a European Union Energy ministers meeting in Brussels on December 3). The draft directive on natural gas deregulation was put back then, but Britain should be there promote its interests".
